lead: Plane stress transformation answers one question: if you know the stresses on a small element aligned with x and y, what are the stresses on the same element after you rotate the axes? The answer is a rotation of the stress tensor. Normal and shear components mix through cos 2θ and sin 2θ. The sum σx + σy does not change. Designers use this to find the worst orientation of a shaft, a pressure vessel or a bracket before choosing a material.
prereq: You need: 2.1 and 2.2, plus basic trigonometry (sin 2θ, cos 2θ).

sections.h3: The stress tensor and a rotation

blocks.text: Plane stress means σz = 0, τxz = 0 and τyz = 0. The element still carries three independent components: σx, σy and τxy. Here σx is the normal stress on the x-face, σy is the normal stress on the y-face, and τxy is the shear stress on the x-face in the y-direction. The tensor is symmetric because τxy = τyx.
Write these components as a 2 × 2 matrix:

blocks.where: S is the plane stress tensor in MPa; σx and σy are normal stresses in MPa; τxy is shear stress in MPa.

blocks.text: Rotate the axes anticlockwise by angle θ to new axes x′ and y′. Use the rotation matrix R = [ [cos θ, sin θ], [−sin θ, cos θ] ]. The new tensor is σ′ = R S Rᵀ, where Rᵀ is the transpose of R. This is the matrix statement of plane stress transformation. It is the same physical element, described in a new coordinate system.
Multiplying the matrices gives three equations. They are the ones used in exams and in design checks.
σx′ = (σx + σy)/2 + (σx − σy)/2 cos 2θ + τxy sin 2θ
blocks.where: σx′ is the normal stress on the new x′-face in MPa; θ is the anticlockwise angle from x to x′ in degrees or radians; other symbols are as above.

blocks.text: σy′ = (σx + σy)/2 − (σx − σy)/2 cos 2θ − τxy sin 2θ
blocks.where: σy′ is the normal stress on the new y′-face in MPa; the same θ and original stresses apply.
τx′y′ is the shear stress on the x′-face in the y′-direction in MPa; positive shear follows the same face-and-direction rule as τxy.

blocks.text: Check the equations at θ = 0: cos 0 = 1, sin 0 = 0, so σx′ = σx, σy′ = σy and τx′y′ = τxy. At θ = 90°, the normal stresses swap and the shear changes sign. The angle 2θ appears because a stress component repeats after a 180° rotation of the element, not after 360°. The force-equilibrium method of 2.2 gives the same result on one inclined plane.
Add the equations for σx′ and σy′. The cos 2θ and sin 2θ terms cancel:

blocks.where: The sum of the two normal stresses is the first invariant of plane stress, in MPa. It is the same in every coordinate system.

blocks.text: This invariant is the trace of the matrix S. The determinant, σxσy − τxy², is a second invariant. The invariant is a check on any rotation calculation: if the sum changes, you made an arithmetic or sign error.
Principal stresses are the eigenvalues of S. They are the two values of λ that satisfy det(S − λI) = 0, where I is the 2 × 2 identity matrix. In equation form:

blocks.where: λ is a principal stress in MPa; the two roots are σ1 and σ2. 2.4 solves for the roots and the principal angles.

blocks.text: Plane strain transformation uses the same rotation idea, but the shear term is γ/2, not γ. See 2.6.

spec.title: Stress components in MPa: σx, σy, τxy
spec.aria: An array compares original stress components with components after a 45 degree rotation and shows the unchanged normal-stress sum.

examples.question: A plane stress state has σx = 100 MPa, σy = 20 MPa and τxy = 40 MPa. Rotate the axes anticlockwise by θ = 45°. Find σx′, σy′ and τx′y′. Check the invariant.
steps: Invariant: σx + σy = 100 + 20 = 120 MPa. Also σx′ + σy′ = 100 + 20 = 120 MPa. The check passes.
examples.answer: σx′ = 100 MPa, σy′ = 20 MPa, τx′y′ = −40 MPa; the invariant sum is 120 MPa.
examples.check:
import math
sx = 100.0
sy = 20.0
txy = 40.0
th = math.radians(45.0)
c = math.cos(2*th)
s = math.sin(2*th)
sxp = (sx+sy)/2 + (sx-sy)/2*c + txy*s
syp = (sx+sy)/2 - (sx-sy)/2*c - txy*s
txpyp = -(sx-sy)/2*s + txy*c
print(sxp)
print(syp)
print(txpyp)
print(sx+sy)

traps: Using θ inside sin 2θ and cos 2θ instead of 2θ. Compute 2θ first, then take sine and cosine.
Assuming a positive τxy gives a positive τx′y′. At θ = 45° in the worked example, τxy = +40 MPa becomes τx′y′ = −40 MPa.
Thinking the invariant fixes each normal stress. Only the sum σx + σy is fixed; σx′ and σy′ can swap or change.
Using the stress equations for strain. For strain, the shear term is γ/2; see 2.6.
Mixing degrees and radians. If θ = 45°, use 90° in the trig functions, not 90 rad.

quiz.a: σx + σy = σx′ + σy′; the sum of normal stresses is unchanged by rotation.

quiz.q: Why does a physical element show different stress components after rotation?
quiz.a: The components are resolved on new faces. The tensor is the same, but the axes change, so normal and shear parts mix through cos 2θ and sin 2θ.

quiz.q: For σx = 80 MPa, σy = 20 MPa, τxy = 0 and θ = 30°, find σx′ and τx′y′.
A student says τxy = 0 means no shear exists on any plane. Is this true? Explain with an equation.
quiz.a: False. τx′y′ = −(σx − σy)/2 sin 2θ. If σx ≠ σy and θ is not 0° or 90°, shear appears on inclined planes even when τxy = 0.

quiz.q: Write the plane stress tensor as a matrix.
What are principal stresses in matrix language?
quiz.a: They are the eigenvalues of the plane stress tensor S, found from det(S − λI) = 0.

quiz.q: For σx = 100 MPa, σy = 20 MPa, τxy = 40 MPa and θ = 45°, what is τx′y′?

beyond: Not for the exam. The same rotation appears in finite element software when it builds element stiffness matrices in local axes. Composite laminates stack plies at different angles, and each ply needs its stresses transformed into its own fibre direction. Strain-gauge rosettes use the inverse idea: measured strains at three angles give the tensor. Search for “stress transformation finite element” or “laminate coordinate transformation”.
